extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York, delegates, and readers considering the proposed federal judiciary (ratifiers and policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and legal-maxims about the organization, jurisdiction, and procedural consequences of the proposed federal judiciary: distribution of original and appellate jurisdiction, relation to State courts, trial-by-jury implications, and institutional safeguards (e.g., impeachment, judicial tenure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature cannot reverse particular judicial sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature, without exceeding its province, cannot reverse a determination once made in a particular case; it may only prescribe a new rule for future cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory of British or State constitutions does not authorize the revisal of a judicial sentence by legislative act; impropriety on principles of law and reason prevents retroactive legislative reversal of individual judicial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute inferior courts is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of constituting inferior courts is evidently calculated to obviate the necessity of having recourse to the Supreme Court in every case of federal cognizance and to enable the national government to institute tribunals competent to determine national matters within States or districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without this power, the Supreme Court would be overburdened; inferior federal tribunals permit local administration of national law and allow appeals to be safely circumscribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts should not be relied on exclusively for federal causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Though State courts may be fit, conferring federal causes to existing State courts may be improper because local spirit or the character of some State tribunals may disqualify them for national jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns include lack of judicial independence (e.g., tenure during pleasure or year-to-year) and danger of giving too wide a door to appeals; direct provision for federal tribunals is preferable in many respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer district-based federal courts over one per State
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be expedient to divide the United States into several districts and institute a federal court in each district, in lieu of one in every State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts, aided by State judges holding circuits, can administer justice with ease and dispatch, and allow appellate jurisdiction to be circumscribed within a narrow compass — this plan is 'most eligible' for practical administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit Supreme Court original jurisdiction to narrow classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court is to be invested with original jurisdiction only 'in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls, and those in which A STATE shall be a party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public ministers and cases where a State is a party concern national peace and dignity and are proper for first-instance decision by the nation's highest judicatory; other federal causes should originate in inferior tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: State sovereignty and immunity from suit without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inherent in the nature of sovereignty not to be amenable to the suit of an individual without its consent; unless surrendered by the plan, States retain this immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts confer no compulsive right of action against a sovereign absent its consent; implying federal courts would authorize suits that could not be enforced (without war) is unwarrantable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction may extend to law and fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court may possess appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact, 'with such exceptions and under such regulations as the Congress shall make.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad grant avoids technical traps (differences in State practice) and permits the national legislature to regulate how facts and law are re-examined (e.g., remand for second jury or issue directed out of the Supreme Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction does not abolish trial by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate jurisdiction, even if extending to matters of fact, does not necessarily abolish the trial by jury; re-examination can be regulated so as not to supersede jury trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress could provide that in appeals there shall be no re-examination of facts tried by juries, or qualify that exclusion to certain kinds of causes; appellate review can be fashioned to preserve jury trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review of facts is review of the record, not de novo fact-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: A superior court taking cognizance of fact 'takes cognizance of it as it appears upon the record, and pronounces the law arising upon it' — it cannot institute a new inquiry concerning the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate jurisdiction of fact often means reviewing the recorded fact; separation between fact and law is not always possible, and appellate fact-review can be limited by procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State courts in federal causes unless expressly excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will retain the jurisdiction they now have unless it appears to be taken away in express terms, and will of course take cognizance of causes arising under the laws of the Union where not expressly prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because national and State systems form 'one whole,' State courts act as natural auxiliaries in executing Union laws; appeals from State courts to the Supreme Court should be allowed to preserve national uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from State courts to Supreme Court should be allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal would certainly lie from State tribunals to the Supreme Court of the United States; the Constitution's grant of appellate jurisdiction contemplates the objects of appeal, not solely the tribunals appealed from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending appeals to include State courts prevents elusion of national authority and secures final determination 'in the courts of the Union' for enumerated classes of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature may establish appeals from State courts to subordinate federal tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is authorized to constitute 'tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court' and may, in its discretion, provide that appeals from State courts lie to subordinate national tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a power could reduce the need to multiply federal courts and allow arrangements that contract the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction, leaving State tribunals more charge of federal causes with appeals to district courts when proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of particulars defines and limits federal judicial power
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial authority of the federal judicatures is declared to comprehend certain cases particularly specified; the expression of those cases marks the precise limits beyond which federal courts cannot extend jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification excludes any pretension to a more general authority; enumerated grants should be read naturally and according to the purpose of the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power to constitute courts includes prescribing trial modes
rubrics_metrics.description: A power to constitute courts is a power to prescribe the mode of trial; where the Constitution is silent as to civil jury trials, the legislature has discretion to adopt or omit that institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressing jury trial for criminal cases does not imply prohibition of jury trial in civil cases; silence is not abolition, and the legislature may choose modes appropriate to different causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial authority should be carefully restricted and balanced by safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial department's authority has been carefully restricted to causes proper for national cognizance; original jurisdiction reserved sparingly for the Supreme Court; appellate jurisdiction is subject to exceptions — impeachment and degradation are constitutional checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comparative weakness of judiciary, exercise manner, and the legislative power of impeachment (trial by Senate) are cited as important constitutional checks that guard against judicial usurpation.
